In [[mathematical logic]], the '''Kanamori–McAloon theorem''', due to {{harvtxt|Kanamori|McAloon|1987}}, gives an example of an [[Complete theory|incompleteness]] in [[Peano arithmetic]], similar to that of the [[Paris–Harrington theorem]]. They showed that a certain finitistic theorem in [[Ramsey theory]] is not provable in Peano arithmetic (PA).

==Statement==
Given a set <math> s\subseteq\mathbb{N} </math> of non-negative integers, let <math>\min(s)</math> denote the [[Maxima and minima|minimum]] element of <math>s</math>. Let <math>[X]^n</math> denote the set of all ''n''-element [[Subset|subsets]] of <math>X</math>.

A function <math>f:[X]^n\rightarrow\mathbb{N}</math> where <math>X\subseteq\mathbb{N}</math> is said to be ''regressive'' if <math>f(s)<\min(s)</math> for all <math>s</math> not containing 0.

The Kanamori–McAloon theorem states that the following proposition, denoted by <math>(*)</math> in the original reference, is not provable in PA:

:For every <math>n,k\in\mathbb{N}</math>, there exists an <math>m\in\mathbb{N}</math> such that for all regressive <math>f:[\{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}]^n\rightarrow\mathbb{N}</math>, there exists a set <math>H\in[\{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}]^k</math> such that for all <math>s,t\in[H]^n</math> with <math>\min(s)=\min(t)</math>, we have <math>f(s)=f(t)</math>.
